title: Quantum incompatibility of Born probabilities
authors: Esteban Castro-Ruiz, Nathan Cohen, Luis C. Barbado, Časlav Brukner
abstract: Quantum theory challenges the view that individual measurement outcomes are predefined and independent of the measurement context. Yet the quantum state itself -- the catalogue of probabilities for all possible measurements -- is usually assumed to be well defined. We argue that this assumption tacitly relies on measurements being performed relative to ideal, infinitely-resourceful reference frames. We show that, when measurements are made relative to non-ideal quantum reference frames, the probabilities themselves become indefinite: even in the limit of arbitrarily large number of runs, the relative frequencies may remain uncertain. The uncertainty is irreducible in a quantum-mechanical sense, as we show by proving a Bell-type theorem for relative frequencies. We further propose a quantum-optical implementation of these relational measurements based on pulsed homodyne detection. Our findings motivate an extension of the notion of the quantum state to regimes constrained by finite resources. We expect them to be especially relevant at the interface between quantum theory and general relativity, where the resources and information available in a bounded region of spacetime are fundamentally limited.
summary: The paper argues that assuming ideal reference frames when calculating probabilities leads to an oversimplification. By analyzing measurements relative to finite-resource Quantum Reference Frames, the authors demonstrate that the resulting relative frequencies are fundamentally uncertain, violating Bell inequalities in the large repetition limit. This suggests a necessary revision of the quantum state concept for regimes constrained by physical resources.
main_problem: The paper investigates how quantum probabilities behave when measurements are performed relative to non-ideal, finite-resource Quantum Reference Frames (QRFs), challenging the assumption that standard Born rules hold universally.
main_result: When reference frames are resource-limited, the relative frequencies themselves become fundamentally indefinite, violating Bell-type inequalities even in the large repetition limit.
method: The authors develop mathematical tools using relative frequency operators and construct CHSH-type correlators to test for compatibility with local hidden variable models.
model_or_system: The model involves a system measured repeatedly (i.i.d. copies) whose measurement context is defined by an auxiliary, physical QRF. This framework is proposed to be implemented using pulsed continuous-variable quantum optics and homodyne detection.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. In ordinary quantum theory, the value of an observable may be uncertain, but the probabilities are sharply defined. The Born rule assigns each outcome a fixed number p = ⟨ψ| P |ψ⟩, and the law of large numbers guarantees that the relative frequencies recorded over N system copies converge to these probabilities as N →∞: individual outcomes may be uncertain, but the statistics governing them are not. This, however, presupposes an ideal reference frame with respect to which the mea- surements are done. When Alice’s QRF A is non-ideal, this is no longer the case. The N →∞limit of the relative frequencies — namely, the Born probabilities — remain uncertain. This figure is a qualitative...

FIG. 2. Alice and Bob perform local experiments on N copies of their systems a and b, respectively, measuring relative frequencies and expectation values with respect to their local reference frames A and B, which may be prepared in a quantum state. Because these frames are non-ideal, the relative frequencies and expectation values they measure may have a finite uncertainty even in the limit of arbitrarily large N. Here we show that these uncertainties are irreducible in a quantum mechanical sense. That is, the correlations between the RRFs or REVs measured by Alice and Bob may violate Bell inequalities in the large-N limit.

FIG. 3. Quantum-optical implementation of the Bell experiment for relational expectation values. Alice and Bob receive a block of N signal modes, a1, . . . , aN and b1, . . . , bN, respectively. The input beam-splitter arrays coherently combine each block into the collective modes cA = N −1/2 PN i=1 ai and cB = N −1/2 PN i=1 bi. With the convention used in the figure, the k-th beam splitter in the input array has intensity transmissivity tk = 1/k, for k = 2, . . . , N, for the newly added input mode into the continuing collective output mode.
